chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

In five qalas (young camels), one sheep; and there is nothing in less than five. In ten, two sheep; in fifteen, three sheep; in twenty, four sheep; in twenty-five, five sheep; and in twenty-six, a bint makhad (a one-year-old female camel) up to thirty.
And Abd al-Rahman said: This is the difference between us and the people. Then he continued the hadith to its end according to what we presented earlier.

key_terms.بِنْتُ مَخَاضٍ: a one-year-old female camel whose mother is nursing
key_terms.قَلَائِصَ: young camels (specifically those in their fourth year)

ai.seo_question: What is the zakat ruling for a herd of twenty-five camels according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the specific *nisab* thresholds for zakat on camels, establishing the precise quantities of sheep or young camels due for herds ranging from five to twenty-five heads. It underscores the distinct juristic methodology of the Shia school, as noted by the narrator, which differentiates its valuation and distribution rules from other Islamic schools. This transmission highlights the systematic approach to livestock taxation rooted in the Imams' teachings, ensuring clarity in religious obligations for the community.
